rows.label: Built for
cells:
Built for: US-formed startups that pay electronically and never handle cash. Founders may live outside the US.
Best fit: when you want a $0 account with free wires and up to $5M of FDIC sweep coverage, and can live with zero interest below $250,000.

Built for: funded startups and growing companies that want corporate cards and spend software with a non-bank cash account.
Best fit: when you have raised money and can hold $50,000, the threshold for the monthly-payments card, run a US entity from a physical US address, and will keep idle cash in Treasury and Vault.

Built for: US-incorporated C-corps and LLCs that want $0-fee checking with a charge card and a treasury product from one provider. A US operating address or a US-based owner is required.
Best fit: when you keep $25,000 or more on the platform, pay vendors by ACH and wire, and want 24/7 phone support without a paid plan.

Built for: US-registered small businesses that want many free checking accounts and plan-based savings interest without a big-bank fee schedule. C-corps and LLCs qualify.
Best fit: a side project or pre-seed company with modest cash whose owners have a physical US address and an SSN or passport, and who value account structure and bookkeeping hand-off over an API or treasury yield.

Built for: US-incorporated startups that want a chartered bank with branches, a business debit card, Ink business credit cards and a route to J.P. Morgan's startup bankers if the company later raises venture money.
Best fit: when a founder can keep $2,000 in the account to waive the fee, lives in the US or can reach a branch, and values a single insured bank over yield.

Built for: US technology and life-science startups that want a chartered bank with venture debt and a named relationship manager.
Best fit: once you hold $15,000 or more on deposit, the Essentials fee-waiver balance, and expect to raise from VCs, so the fee waiver, money market tiers and in-house lending all apply.

No product at all: you open a plain business checking account at an FDIC-insured bank or credit union and do the rest yourself. You split cash across banks to stay under $250,000 at each, buy Treasury bills through TreasuryDirect or a brokerage for yield, and connect QuickBooks or Xero to the bank feed. It suits US-resident founders at the side-project or pre-seed stage who hold under $250,000 and make a handful of payments a month.

rows.label: 1. What it is
cells: Mercury is a fintech, not a bank. Your deposits sit at Choice Financial Group and Column N.A., and Patriot Bank issues its IO charge card. Founded in 2017, it raised a $200M Series D at a $5.2B valuation in May 2026 and says more than 300,000 customers use it. Its own bank, Mercury Bank, N.A., has preliminary conditional OCC approval (April 2026) and conditional FDIC approval (September 2026), with Federal Reserve approval still needed and an opening projected for 2027.

Brex is a fintech, not a chartered bank. Since 7 April 2026 Brex LLC has been a wholly owned subsidiary of Capital One; the deal was announced in January 2026 at $5.15 billion. It was founded in 2017 by Henrique Dubugras and Pedro Franceschi; Franceschi stays CEO. Your money sits elsewhere: checking is a deposit account at Column N.A., Vault balances are swept across program banks by Brex Treasury LLC, and Treasury money buys shares of a government money market fund. The January 2026 announcement cited over 25,000 companies.

Rho is a fintech, not a bank, founded in New York in 2018. Checking and cards are provided by Webster Bank (a division of Santander Bank) and by Lead Bank; savings balances are swept to a network of banks run by American Deposit Management. Webster stopped being a separate bank on 20 August 2026, when Banco Santander closed its $12.2 billion purchase of Webster Financial. Rho Treasury is a separate brokerage product run by an SEC-registered adviser and is not FDIC insured. Current customer count and deposits are not disclosed.

Relay is a financial technology company, not a bank. Deposits sit at Thread Bank, an FDIC-insured community bank in Tennessee that also issues the Relay Visa cards. Relay runs the app, the multi-account structure and integrations. Founded in 2018 and headquartered in Toronto under co-founder and CEO Yoseph West, it took $50 million from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund in May 2026 after a $32.2 million Series B in May 2024, and reported more than 150,000 customers and $1.3 billion in deposits at that date.

Chase is the consumer and small-business brand of JPMorgan Chase Bank. It is a nationally chartered bank that holds your deposits itself; FDIC records show it was established in 1824 and held $4.09 trillion in assets, $2.82 trillion in deposits and 5,402 offices as of 30 June 2026. Separately, J.P. Morgan's commercial bank runs an Innovation Economy practice for venture-backed companies that reported 12,000 clients and 550 or more bankers (September 2026).

Silicon Valley Bank is a division of a chartered bank, not a fintech. Since 27 March 2023 it has operated inside First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company. That bank bought the failed bank's assets and deposits from the FDIC, and your deposits sit directly there with no partner-bank layer. First Citizens announced in April 2026 that it will retire the SVB name during Q4 2026, when the technology and healthcare business becomes First Citizens Innovation Banking; as of 5 October 2026 svb.com still carries the old name.

The internal build is not a product. You open a plain business checking account at an FDIC-insured bank or credit union and then do by hand what the fintech accounts bundle. Coverage is the FDIC's standard $250,000 per depositor, per bank, so insuring more means more banks, or asking your bank for IntraFi's ICS or CDARS. For yield you buy Treasury bills through a TreasuryDirect entity account (no fees, $100 minimum) or a brokerage; the 13-week bill auctioned on 5 October 2026 cleared at 4.149%. Budgets live in a spreadsheet and accounting runs on a QuickBooks or Xero bank feed.

rows.label: 2. Eligibility & onboarding
cells: Open to US-formed companies with US operations even if the founders live abroad. The FAQ (read 5 October 2026) allows a residential or international principal address but not a registered agent, P.O. box or UPS box, and excludes founders in listed countries; in July 2024 it closed accounts in Nigeria and other African countries. You upload formation documents, the EIN letter and a passport or other ID for owners of 25% or more; the FAQ does not say a passport fully replaces an SSN. No minimum, no branch, and 10 minutes or less to open.

You need a US-registered entity with an EIN plus US operations and a US physical address. C-corp, S-corp, LLC and LLP entities qualify, PO boxes are refused, and sole proprietorships are not on the list. With a virtual registration address, an owner must be verifiable at a US address. Owners of 25% or more give a taxpayer ID, or a passport number without an SSN. Brex's last official word on founders abroad is a 2021 post; a Trustpilot reviewer in May 2026 reports a US residential address is now required. The monthly-payments card needs $50,000 in cash for funded startups; checking has no stated minimum.

US-incorporated entities only. Rho's help center asks for either a US operating address or one owner based in the US with an SSN, while its own guide (October 2026) wants at least one US-based owner or officer and a physical US operating address; the two pages differ, so ask Rho which rule applies. Founders without an SSN are verified by passport, and sole proprietors are not accepted. Rho will also incorporate you, a Delaware C-corp for $400 or an LLC for $349. The terms let Rho close accounts at any time without notice.

Relay opens accounts for US-registered LLCs and corporations as well as general partnerships and sole proprietorships. Corporations can be C corp or S corp; nothing registered outside the United States qualifies. The business address must be physical, with no PO boxes or virtual mailboxes. Founders abroad are accepted when the business has an operating presence in the US, but every beneficial owner must give a physical US address, and the two onboarding pages disagree on whether a passport number can replace an SSN (both updated August 2026). Most applications are reviewed within 1 to 2 business days, with no minimum balance.

Chase accepts sole proprietorships, LLCs, corporations and partnerships; corporations need an EIN. Only sole proprietors, corporations and single-member or single-manager LLCs can apply online; a multi-member LLC applies in a branch with every member or manager present. Each owner of 10% or more gives a residential address and a tax identification number, and non-permanent residents can show a passport as primary ID. The business pages do not say whether a foreign address, a registered agent or a virtual office is accepted, so a founder living abroad should expect a branch visit.

SVB banks technology, life science and healthcare companies from pre-seed upward, and there is no self-serve signup: you submit a web form and a team member reaches out, with no published time to open. Current pages do not state SSN, ITIN or address rules; a 2021 sheet from before the First Citizens purchase says no US SSN or ITIN is required, so confirm it with the bank. The client FAQ says SVB serves non-US clients on a cross-border basis from the United States. No minimum balance to open and no branch visit, since SVB accounts are not serviced in First Citizens branches.

Any US entity with an EIN can apply. Each bank sets its own rules. Bank of America says applicants should be US residents and that foreign business customers are unable to apply, and asks for an SSN for everyone on the application, including every owner at 25% or more. Wells Fargo requires a physical address, rejects registered agents, virtual addresses and PO or commercial mailboxes, accepts a passport as primary ID and prefers all owners present at opening. Minimum opening deposits are $25 at Wells Fargo and $0 at Bank of America. None of the bank pages describes a path for a founder living outside the US.

rows.label: 3. Fees & minimums
cells: $0 a month on the Mercury plan (as of 5 October 2026). Plus is $29.90 and Pro $299, with no minimum balance and no overdraft or opening fees. ACH and domestic wires are free both ways; USD international wires are free with SHA charging or $15 with OUR, and non-USD wires carry a 1% conversion fee. Card spend in other currencies costs up to 3%, and cash deposits are not accepted.

$0 per user per month on Essentials and $12 on Premium (as of 5 October 2026). Enterprise is custom-priced. The fee schedule lists $0.00 for ACH, checks, and domestic and international wires in both directions, and no opening, maintenance, minimum or overdraft fees. What does cost money: an FX markup of up to 3% on card spend in other currencies, $15 for principal protection on an international USD wire, and a late card payment at 2.99% or $38. No cash deposits and no ATM withdrawals.

$0 subscription and $0 per user on a single plan (as of 5 October 2026). Same-day ACH, domestic wires and mailed checks are free too. Rho Platinum, which raises card cashback, is earned rather than paid: keep 50% or more of company assets at Rho, run payroll from it and hold an active card. The fees that exist are a 1% conversion on non-USD transfers, an optional $15 to cover SWIFT charges, a $30 recall on international wires, and a Treasury wrap fee of 0.60% a year under $2 million, falling to 0.15% at $20 million. No cash deposits or ATM access.

$0 a month on Starter (as of 17 September 2026). Grow is $30 and Scale $90, the last discounted from a regular $120. No minimum balance and no overdraft fees. Standard ACH is free; same-day ACH costs $1, $0.50 or nothing by plan; outgoing domestic wires $8, $5 or $5; SWIFT wires $25, $22 or $20. Incoming wires are listed at $5 in the deposit agreement but free in one help article, so confirm. Paper checks are free, cash deposits are free at Allpoint+ ATMs, and closing costs nothing.

$15 a month for Business Complete Checking (fee schedule effective 14 June 2026). The fee is $0 with a $2,000 minimum daily balance, $2,000 of Ink card spend, or a linked Chase Private Client account, and the first two months are waived. Electronic deposits, ACH, ATM use and debit card purchases cost nothing; banker transactions and paper checks are free for the first 20 a month, then $0.50 each. Cash is free at ATMs and free to $5,000 a month at a branch. No closing fee is listed.

$25 a month for Essentials Checking (as of 5 October 2026). The fee is waived when the monthly average balance across your accounts is $15,000 or more. Included at no charge: 15 outgoing wires a month (5 domestic, 5 international USD, 5 international FX), ACH received, standard checks, bill pay and mobile deposit; ACH you originate is not included. Outside the bundle the fee schedule lists $32 standard maintenance, $0.15 per ACH item and $30 daily overdrafts up to $150 a day, all described as minimums that may vary by client.

$15 to $16 a month for entry-level checking at the big banks (with waivers). Wells Fargo Initiate is $15, waived with a $2,000 minimum daily balance or $5,000 average combined balance, with 100 free transactions then $0.50 each (schedule effective 28 July 2026). Bank of America Fundamentals is $16, waived with a $5,000 average balance or $500 of debit card purchases a cycle, and not charged until the thirteenth statement cycle (schedule effective 20 February 2026).

rows.label: 4. Yield & treasury
cells: Checking and savings pay 0.00% APY under the Column deposit agreement (August 2026). Yield comes only from Mercury Treasury, which needs $250,000 across your Mercury accounts: as of 2 October 2026 the net tiers start at 3.15% in a government money market fund or 3.55% in an ultra-short bond fund, and the headline 4.00% applies above $20M. The fee is 0.15% to 0.6% a year. Treasury balances are securities, not deposits: not FDIC insured, SIPC covered to $500,000.

Checking pays nothing; the fee schedule lists uninvested cash as no yield. Treasury buys shares of the BNY Dreyfus Government Cash Management fund with no minimum, and the posted total return is 3.56% under $500K, 3.61% to $2M, 3.71% to $5M, 3.76% to $20M and 3.91% above, as of 5 October 2026; Brex lowered these tiers from 4.01% to 4.36% on 2 October 2026. Moves back to checking take as little as an hour. Treasury holdings are securities: not FDIC insured, SIPC covered to $500,000.

The sources used here do not state a checking rate. Rho Business Savings pays up to 1.00% as of August 2026, needs $25,000 and allows six transfers out a month. The higher yield is Rho Treasury, a brokerage account with a $50,000 minimum: for $50,000 to $2 million the net yields were 3.55% on 13-week Treasury bills (5 October 2026) and 3.21% on a money market fund (2 October 2026), rising to 4.00% on bills at $20 million or more. Holdings are SIPC protected to $500,000 and not FDIC insured. The homepage still advertised up to 4.57% in August 2026, so check the live rate.

Only savings accounts earn interest, and the rate is a plan feature: 1.19% APY on Starter, 1.87% on Grow and 3.21% on Scale as of 17 September 2026, variable and paid monthly, with no minimum. Checking earns nothing. Because yield is bought with the subscription, Scale at $90 a month only beats Starter above roughly $53,500 of average savings balance. There is no treasury or money-market product: every balance is a bank deposit inside the FDIC sweep, so large idle cash that wants Treasury bill yield needs a separate brokerage account.

Business Complete Checking does not earn interest, and the business rate sheet in effect on 2 October 2026 shows Business Total Savings at 0.01% APY and Business Premier Savings at 0.02%. The only deposit yields near market rates are the featured relationship CDs: as of 2 October 2026 the 7-month CD paid 3.50% APY under $100,000 and 4.00% above, with a $1,000 minimum and an early withdrawal penalty. End-of-day sweeps are not permitted on Business Complete Checking, and the J.P. Morgan startups page names liquidity management but states no yield, minimum or fee.

Checking is non-interest bearing. Yield comes from the Startup Money Market Account: 3.56% APY on balances above $1,000,000, 2.63% on $50,000.01 to $1,000,000 and 0.10% on $50,000 or less, as of 30 September 2026, only while you hold the tier balance; it is a bank deposit, FDIC-insured to $250,000. For larger balances there are two sweeps: SVB Cash Sweep moves idle cash into money market mutual funds from BlackRock, Morgan Stanley and Western Asset, which are investments, not deposits, and Insured Cash Sweep through IntraFi places cash below $250,000 at other network banks.

Plain checking pays nothing or close to it: Wells Fargo Initiate and Bank of America Fundamentals are non-interest-bearing, and Navy Federal Business Checking earns 0.01% APY. Yield is what you buy yourself. On 5 October 2026 the 4-week Treasury bill stood at 3.95% and the 13-week at 4.15%; bills come in 4 to 52-week terms, $100 minimum, with no fee at TreasuryDirect, and Fidelity charges $0 for Treasury orders placed online. There is no management fee because there is no manager; the cost is your time.

rows.label: 5. FDIC coverage & safety
cells: Up to $5M of FDIC coverage on the free plan comes from sweeping deposits across up to 20 banks. It is pass-through insurance: it pays if an insured bank fails, not if Mercury fails, and Treasury balances are not covered. An industry tracker lists Choice Financial Group under an FDIC consent order dated December 2023, and former partner Evolve Bank & Trust received a Federal Reserve order in June 2024. Freeze and closure reports recur: 21% of 2,839 Trustpilot reviews are one-star (5 October 2026).

Checking at Column N.A. is insured to $250,000 combined across all sub-accounts. Vault is a sweep run by Brex Treasury LLC across program banks and advertises up to $6M of coverage (5 October 2026); the published list names 27 banks while the product page says 24. Treasury money is never FDIC insured. Brex has dropped customers before: in June 2022 it told tens of thousands of small businesses to leave, and 2026 Trustpilot reviews report a closure without warning and a credit limit cut to zero overnight.

Checking at Webster Bank or Lead Bank is insured to $250,000 per customer across all Rho checking accounts. Savings is a sweep administered by American Deposit Management that spreads balances in increments below $250,000 across 400+ insured institutions, for up to $75 million of coverage (August 2026). Rho states that FDIC insurance does not protect you against the failure of Rho, and Treasury is not FDIC insured. The terms allow suspension without notice; Trustpilot reviews from late 2025 describe $300,000 held for weeks, and 53 reviews score 3.4 with 26% one-star (5 October 2026).

Deposits sit at Thread Bank, which uses IntraFi to spread balances above $250,000 across program banks for coverage up to $3,000,000. Each program bank holds up to $250,000, every customer is enrolled automatically, and the balance still shows as one number in the app. Thread Bank was under an FDIC consent order from May 2024 until the FDIC terminated it in December 2025. The deposit agreement lets the bank suspend or close your account with or without notice and pays out closed accounts by paper check. Trustpilot one-star reviews from July to September 2026 report closures without explanation and funds held for up to 45 days.

Deposits sit directly at JPMorgan Chase Bank with the standard $250,000 of coverage and no sweep on the standard business accounts. The FDIC limit is per depositor, per bank, per ownership category; Chase's own explainer says a corporation's accounts at the bank are combined under the limit, so a C-corp with $1 million in Chase checking and savings has $250,000 insured and $750,000 uninsured. No 2023 or 2024 failure event touched Chase deposits. Chase's Trustpilot profile shows a 1.3 TrustScore from 2,864 reviews, 89% one-star over the prior 12 months (5 October 2026), though it mixes consumer and business complaints.

Deposits are held directly at First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company, so standard coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category; balances above that are uninsured unless you enrol in Insured Cash Sweep. The predecessor bank failed: it was closed on 10 March 2023 with more than 85% of deposits uninsured, and the FDIC used a systemic risk exception so that all depositors were made whole. The deposit agreement allows the bank to close, freeze or suspend any account without notice; no wider pattern of freeze reports was found.

Coverage is the FDIC's standard $250,000 per depositor at each insured bank. A corporation's deposits at one bank are combined under that cap however many owners sign, and each extra bank carries its own $250,000, which is why splitting works; IntraFi's ICS and CDARS do the splitting through one bank, with depositor fees its pages do not publish. The March 2023 bank failure showed both the limit and the discretion in the deposit route: the FDIC made all depositors whole under a systemic risk exception, a discretionary act, not a rule.

rows.label: 6. Cards, credit & spend controls
cells: The IO card is a charge card from Patriot Bank with no personal guarantee. It has no annual fee, no late fee and unlimited 1.5% cashback; you repay daily until balances reach $15K, then can switch to 30-day terms, and non-USD spend costs 3.00%. Admins get virtual cards, per-person limits and merchant-locked cards. Venture debt from Mercury Lending is for companies that raised venture capital in the last 12 months, and is not offered in California.

Cards are Visa or Mastercard cards issued by Emigrant Bank or Fifth Third Bank. Daily payments track your available balance; monthly payments run a 30-day statement and need $50,000 in cash if you have raised money. There is no personal guarantee, and limits are set on revenue and cash balance rather than a personal credit score. Points are 7x on rideshare, 4x on Brex-booked travel, 3x at restaurants, 2x on recurring software and 1x elsewhere, redeemed at 0.6 cents per point in cash. Unlimited virtual cards come on the $0 plan; expense policies need Premium at $12 per user.

The Rho Corporate Card is a Mastercard World Elite charge card issued by Lead Bank or Webster Bank. The full balance is repaid each period. Every account starts on Daily Terms; Monthly Terms opens once you hold $25,000 at Rho or $75,000 including linked accounts. No personal guarantee, no personal credit pull. Cashback is 1.25% on Daily Terms and 1% on Monthly Terms, up to 2% and 1.75% with Rho Platinum, on up to $1,000,000 of spend a year; non-US transactions earn nothing. Rho Capital is a revolving line from Lead Bank of up to $5 million that needs consent to a personal credit report. There is no venture debt.

Both cards are Visa cards issued by Thread Bank. Debit cards run up to 50 per cardholder per checking account with per-card limits and category controls; non-US card transactions cost 1%. The Relay Visa Credit Card is a charge card with a 30-day cycle, no annual fee, a 1% foreign transaction fee and cash back of 1% on Starter, 1.25% on Grow and 1.5% on Scale. No credit-score check at application, but eligibility is revenue-based: $50,000 or more in average monthly revenue with 12 months in business, or $20,000 with 6 months and $25,000 held at Relay. There is no line of credit or venture debt.

Business Complete Checking comes with a debit card ($10,000 daily purchase limit) and employee debit access through the Business Associate Card at $0 annual fee. Credit is the Ink line (5 October 2026): Ink Business Unlimited has a $0 annual fee and 1.5% cash back;; Ink Business Premier costs $195 with 2% back and 2.5% on purchases of $5,000 or more. The Ink Business Unlimited terms make you and the business jointly responsible for the balance. A line of credit of $10,000 to $500,000 needs $100,000 in annual revenue, a FICO score of at least 660 and a personal guarantee from 20% owners.

Business checking comes with a Mastercard debit card; foreign debit transactions carry a 2.00% assessment. The credit product for early-stage and Series A companies is the Innovator Card, a charge card issued by First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company, marketed with higher limits and no personal liability: $0 annual fee, a 0 to 3% foreign currency fee, a late fee of the greater of $32 or 2.5% of the balance, and 1.5X points on all spend with no cap (terms revised May 2026). SVB's own article sizes venture debt at 25 to 35% of the last equity round.

The deposit accounts come with a business debit card and employee debit cards and nothing else. There is no charge card, no cashback and no virtual cards; business credit cards and lines of credit are separate applications whose terms the sources used here do not state. Bank of America's employee debit cards default to a $400 daily purchase limit, adjustable to $7,500; Wells Fargo lets you adjust daily limits and turn a card on or off. That is the whole control surface: a daily cap and a switch, with no category blocks, merchant locks or receipt matching.

rows.label: 7. Payments & international
cells: Every rail costs $0: ACH, domestic wires in and out, real-time payments and mailed checks (5 October 2026), and Mercury says 99.6% of domestic payments sent in 2025 arrived within one business day. USD international wires are free with SHA charging or $15 with OUR; non-USD wires convert at 1% into 40+ currencies across 200+ countries. FedNow is not mentioned. Bill pay supports approval rules so creators cannot approve their own payments. No cash deposits.

Every rail is $0 as of 5 October 2026: ACH in both directions, checks, and domestic and international wires in and out. ACH started before 3:15 pm ET leaves the same day; wires cut off at 4 pm ET. The wires page lists 123 destination countries, and Brex sets the FX rate on non-USD wires at its sole discretion without stating the margin. The pages do not mention RTP or FedNow, do not state ACH or wire limits, and there are no cash deposits or ATM withdrawals.

Domestic payments are free: same-day ACH, standard ACH, domestic wires and mailed checks all cost $0 (5 October 2026). ACH created before 2 pm ET and under $1 million settles the same day. Limits are high: $20 million a day in ACH, $90 million in domestic wires and $2.5 million in international wires. International payments run through Wise US Inc. to over 200 countries in 23 currencies; USD wires carry no Rho fee, non-USD transfers pay 1%, and recalls cost $30. Eight countries are blocked and 52 more restricted. RTP and FedNow are not mentioned.

Standard ACH is free on every plan and takes 1 to 2 business days; same-day ACH costs $1, $0.50 or nothing by plan with a 4:15 pm ET cutoff, and limits are set per account rather than published. Outgoing domestic wires ($8, $5 or $5) usually arrive within one business day; SWIFT wires ($25, $22 or $20) go out in 2 to 3 business days; local-network wires ($5, $3 or $1.50) reach EUR, GBP, CAD or AUD. Non-USD conversion starts at 1% and accounts hold USD only. Zelle is not supported and RTP or FedNow are not mentioned.

Wires are priced like a traditional bank (fee schedule effective 14 June 2026): incoming wires cost $15, or $0 if the sender used Chase; outgoing domestic wires cost $25 online or $35 in a branch; outgoing international wires cost $40 online in US dollars, $5 in a foreign currency or $50 in a branch, with an exchange spread Chase does not quantify. Standard ACH, ATM and debit transactions are free, but the optional ACH Payments service costs $2.50 per item for the first 10 a month, and Same Day ACH and Real Time Payments each cost 1% of the amount up to $25.

Essentials includes 15 outgoing wires a month and incoming ACH at no charge; beyond that, incoming wires cost $10, domestic outgoing wires $12 online, USD and FX international wires $25, intermediary bank charges $35 and a recall $30. ACH is $0.15 per item plus a $5 same-day premium and a $40 monthly online ACH service fee. Same-day ACH runs to $1 million per transaction, next-day ACH to $99.9 million, and real-time payments on the RTP network to $10 million per transfer; FedNow is not mentioned.

Wires are the expensive part. Wells Fargo charges $30 for an outgoing domestic wire or an international wire in US dollars sent online and $40 for any wire sent in a branch (schedule effective 28 July 2026); Bank of America charges $30 outgoing domestic, $45 outgoing international and $15 incoming either way (schedule effective 20 February 2026). Foreign-currency wires carry no wire fee at either bank, which earn on the exchange rate instead and do not publish the markup. ACH limits, RTP or FedNow and multi-step approvals are not stated for the entry-level accounts.

rows.label: 8. Integrations & accounting
cells: Direct integrations with QuickBooks Online, Xero and NetSuite plus CSV export; the QuickBooks and Xero automations are free, while NetSuite categorizations sit on the $299 Pro plan. Mercury Books, launched in September 2026, is built-in bookkeeping at $35 a month, free through 2026. The API covers accounts, payments, cards, invoicing and Treasury, with webhooks, OAuth2 and a sandbox. No native Stripe, Gusto or Rippling connector is stated.

Accounting syncs are included on the $0 Essentials plan: QuickBooks Online and Desktop, Xero, NetSuite, Sage Intacct and Dynamics 365, plus startup ledgers such as Puzzle and Rillet. Payroll connections include Gusto, Rippling, ADP, Paychex and Deel; Stripe does not appear. The API covers accounting, budgets, expenses, payments and transactions, with webhooks, though on 21 September 2026 Brex's status page recorded an unexpected invalidation of some API tokens. Checking supports up to 512 sub-accounts, and reports export as XLSX, CSV, HTML or TXT.

Native accounting syncs: NetSuite, QuickBooks Online, Sage Intacct and Puzzle; Xero connects by bank feed. Payroll listings are Gusto, BambooHR and Workday, and Stripe and Rippling do not appear. The REST API is open to every customer with no waitlist and no fee, but it is read-only: tokens cannot initiate payments, and webhooks and write endpoints are planned but not available (October 2026). You can create multiple operating accounts under one entity, and an External Accountant role gives reconciliation access without the ability to act.

Relay connects directly to QuickBooks Online and Xero for bank feeds and bill pay. Hubdoc and Dext take receipts, and the sweep is invisible to accounting because one monthly statement covers every program bank position. Gusto is the direct payroll connection, and Plaid links Relay to Shopify, Square, Stripe, PayPal and Wise. Structure is the main feature: up to 20 checking accounts on Starter and Grow, 50 on Scale, unlimited users, six preset roles including Read Only, and advisor logins for accountants.

Chase shares account data with third-party apps through tokenized links: you sign in at Chase, the app never sees your password, and you can revoke access at any time. The data-sharing page does not name QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, Stripe, Gusto or Rippling, so no native sync is confirmed. Inside Chase Business Online, Access & Security Manager lets the owner assign permissions and delegate cash management to staff, which is the route for an accountant. The developer portal returned only a page heading on 5 October 2026, so no business API is confirmed.

SVB Go is the online banking platform; it imports balances and transactions into accounting software each night and offers an ERP plugin for NetSuite, Sage Intacct and Microsoft Dynamics. Bill Pay Plus includes standard sync with QuickBooks or Xero at $50 or $250 a month; advanced sync with NetSuite or Intacct adds $50 or $100 a month plus a $1,000 implementation fee. Statements and transactions export as CSV, OFX, QBO, QFX, PDF and BAI. API Banking covers same-day ACH, wires, real-time balances and virtual card issuance, with Plaid and Modern Treasury as partners; webhooks and a direct Stripe or Gusto link are not shown.

The bank feed is the integration. Xero pulls transactions daily and names Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Capital One and Citibank among its direct feeds; QuickBooks says bank and card transactions sync automatically. Stripe and payroll providers pay in by ACH like anyone else, and there is no API, no webhooks and no programmatic access on the deposit side. Sub-accounts are physical accounts, with budget envelopes beyond that in a spreadsheet you maintain. Reconciliation is not automatic: both products describe the feed as automatic, but matching it to statements each month is still a manual task.

rows.label: 9. Lock-in & migration
cells: Leaving is thinly documented: the Column agreement returns a closed account's balance by ACH or paper check and lists no closure fee, and statements, CSV downloads and the API carry your data. The bigger risk is partner-bank changes that alter routing details: the Evolve exit announced in March 2025 moved customers in cohorts over months, and the planned Mercury Bank anticipates transitioning customers from the partner banks once it opens. Switching in comes with an implementation team.

Leaving is self-serve from Company Settings: you ACH the balance to an account in the exact legal or DBA name on file after money market funds liquidate in 1 to 2 business days. No closure fee is stated, and read-only dashboard access is never revoked. Checking sits at Column N.A. under routing number 121145349, and a removed program bank simply has your deposits moved to other program banks. What Capital One ownership means for future partner banks and account numbers is not stated.

Closing is a support request rather than a button: the account owner asks by phone, chat or email after settling any card balance, moving savings to checking and selling Treasury holdings. Export statements and the CSV first, because dashboard access ends at closure; the balance returns by wire or check with no fee. One partner bank has already changed owners, Webster into Santander on 20 August 2026 with accounts unchanged, and whether routing numbers would change in a future switch is not stated.

Closing is free but manual: you cannot close from inside the app, so you move the balance to $0, download the statements you want and contact support; after closure you lose access permanently, including transaction history. Cancelling a paid plan drops you to Starter with accounts and integrations intact. Two things raise the cost of moving: there is no API, so exports are CSV and OFX files, and a bank-initiated closure pays any balance above $1.00 by paper check. Whether account numbers would change if Relay switched partner banks is not stated.

Leaving is manual with no stated exit fee, and because Chase is itself the insured bank there is no sponsor-bank relationship that could change hands behind your account. The downside is that you re-point every payer and vendor yourself; Chase's switch guide lists five steps. Contractual hooks: the business checking bonus (15 September 2026 to 21 January 2027) pays only if the account is open and unrestricted. How long Chase takes to return funds when it closes an account itself is not stated.

Leaving is a conventional bank process: any signer can request closure, it takes effect 30 days after notice, accrued fees may be deducted, there is no closure fee, and the balance comes back by any means the bank chooses, including a check. Because deposits sit directly at First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company there is no partner-bank rotation that would change account numbers. The practical lock-in is the relationship products: the $15,000 waiver balance, money market tiers that pay 2.63% only above $50,000, the Innovator Card and any covenants on venture debt.

Lock-in is low in structure and high in labor. Your account numbers belong to the bank you chose, so they never change because a software vendor swapped partner banks; they change only if you change banks, when every payroll run, Stripe payout and vendor autopay must be re-pointed by hand. Neither the Wells Fargo nor the Bank of America schedule lists a closure fee, and Bank of America charges no monthly fee in the first year, so a first-year exit costs nothing. Treasury bills bought at TreasuryDirect can be moved to a broker to sell early, normally for a fee; holding to maturity avoids it.

rows.label: 10. Maturity, trust & support
cells: Mercury is venture-backed and profitable. It raised a $300M Series C at $3.5B in March 2025 and a $200M Series D at $5.2B in May 2026, reports $650M of annualized revenue (Q3 2025) and has four consecutive profitable years. Support is in-app messaging and email with no phone number published; the $299 Pro plan adds a relationship manager. Trustpilot shows 4.0 from 2,839 reviews (5 October 2026), 67% five-star and 21% one-star, with Mercury replying to 96% of negative reviews.

Brex was founded in 2017 and raised over $1.5 billion at a peak $12.3 billion valuation in January 2022. It cut 282 staff in January 2024 and reached an estimated $700 million of annualized revenue by August 2025 (Sacra). FINRA fined Brex Treasury LLC $900,000 (August 2024) for 2020 to 2021 anti-money-laundering failures in account onboarding. Support is 24/7 by chat, email, phone, SMS and WhatsApp. Trustpilot shows a TrustScore of 1.9 from 575 reviews (5 October 2026); 73% of lifetime reviews are five-star, but only 13 were posted in the last 12 months and the score weights recent reviews.

Founded in 2018 and privately held: a $15 million Series A (January 2021), a $75 million Series B (December 2021) and a $100 million debt facility; profitability, headcount and customer counts are not disclosed. No enforcement action against Rho was found, the status page showed no incidents from 21 September to 5 October 2026, and Rho says it is SOC 2 Type 2 audited every year. Support is phone, email and in-app chat, staffed around the clock every day of the year, on the $0 plan. Trustpilot shows 3.4 from 53 reviews (5 October 2026); NerdWallet rated it 4.3 of 5 in January 2026.

Relay was founded in 2018 in Toronto and is still private; revenue and profitability are undisclosed. No enforcement action against Relay itself was found, but partner Thread Bank was under an FDIC consent order from May 2024 to December 2025. Support is in-app chat with no published hours or response targets; priority support is Scale-only, and the Trustpilot profile lists phone support 9am to 8pm EST on weekdays. Trustpilot shows 4.3 from 3,738 reviews (5 October 2026), 82% five-star and 11% one-star; one-star reviews describe closures without explanation and funds held for weeks.

The bank dates to 1824 and held $4.09 trillion in assets across 5,402 offices as of 30 June 2026. Under a consent order dated March 2024 the OCC fined it $250 million, with a further $98.2 million from the Federal Reserve, for trading-surveillance failures between 2014 and 2023; the OCC terminated its order in March 2026. Downdetector logged more than 3,700 reports of the mobile app down on 1 May 2026, and online banking went down again on 31 May 2026. Trustpilot shows a 1.3 TrustScore from 2,864 reviews, 89% one-star over the prior 12 months (5 October 2026).

The brand dates from 1983 and the owner is First Citizens BancShares. That listed bank holding company had $236.8 billion of assets and $173.4 billion of deposits as of 30 June 2026. No enforcement action against First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company in 2025 or 2026 and no major outage of SVB Go were found. Support is phone and email from 5:00 am to 5:30 pm Pacific on weekdays, with 24-hour login support, and clients keep their relationship managers through the rebrand. Public reviews are thin: Trustpilot shows 2.0 from 12 reviews, the latest from November 2025.

The institutions are old and regulated but the route itself has no vendor. No one is accountable for the combination except you. Pick the bank with its record in mind: the Federal Reserve lifted the 2018 asset growth restriction on Wells Fargo in June 2025 while saying the other provisions of the 2018 enforcement action remain in place. Support runs through branches and phone lines; the sources used here do not measure response times. Public review scores for the big banks are poor and mostly retail: Trustpilot shows Bank of America at 1.4 from 3,665 reviews and Wells Fargo at 1.2 from 1,608 (5 October 2026).

rows.label: 11. Where it stands out
cells:
Payments cost nothing on a $0 plan. ACH, domestic wires, USD international wires with SHA charging, real-time payments and mailed checks are all free (5 October 2026).
The same free plan sweeps deposits across up to 20 banks for up to $5M of FDIC coverage with no minimum balance. The IO charge card pays 1.5% cashback with no personal guarantee, founders abroad have a documented path, and developers get an API with webhooks and a sandbox.

Every payment rail is $0 and the card needs no personal guarantee. Wires in and out, same-day ACH and checks all cost nothing as of 5 October 2026, with no opening or maintenance fee.
Insured capacity comes with yield behind it: $250,000 at Column N.A., a Vault sweep to up to $6M, and Treasury paying 3.56% to 3.91% with no minimum. The card and software bundle costs $0 per user, with unlimited virtual cards, accounting sync, API access and bill pay on Essentials.

There is nothing to pay on the account itself. Monthly fees, per-user fees, same-day ACH, domestic wires and mailed checks are all $0, and USD international wires are free too (5 October 2026).
Human support runs 24/7 by phone, chat and email on that $0 plan, and payment limits reach $20 million a day in ACH. Savings sweeps to $75 million of FDIC coverage across 400+ institutions, the charge card pays up to 2% cashback under Rho Platinum with no personal guarantee, and the read-only API is open to every customer.

Account structure costs nothing. You get up to 20 checking accounts on the $0 Starter plan and 50 on Scale, two savings accounts, unlimited users and advisor logins for accountants, with no minimum balance (17 September 2026).
The sweep reports as one statement, so splitting cash for taxes, payroll and runway does not complicate bookkeeping. Payments on the free tier are cheap, with standard ACH free, domestic wires $8 and free paper checks, and the IntraFi sweep through Thread Bank covers deposits to $3,000,000 automatically.

Deposits sit at a single chartered bank with no partner bank or sweep program behind them. It holds $2.82 trillion in deposits across 5,402 offices, and the $15 fee disappears with $2,000 in the account or $2,000 of Ink spend.
New business checking customers can earn $400 with a $2,000 deposit or $500 with $10,000 held 60 days (offer valid to 21 January 2027). The credit path is wide: Ink Business Unlimited has a $0 annual fee and 1.5% cash back, Ink Business Premier pays 2%, and a line of credit runs from $10,000 to $500,000. A company that grows into a priced round has an in-house path to the Innovation Economy practice.

A chartered bank with a startup product. Deposits sit directly at an FDIC-insured bank with $236.8 billion of assets, and the Startup Money Market Account pays 3.56% APY above $1 million (30 September 2026).
It pays 2.63% between $50,000.01 and $1 million, and Insured Cash Sweep is available for multimillion-dollar coverage. Wires are bundled for an early team: 15 outgoing wires a month at no charge, including 5 international FX wires, with the $25 fee waived above a $15,000 average balance. Credit and lending are in-house: the Innovator Card is a $0 annual fee charge card marketed with no personal liability, and the same bank writes venture debt.

No platform layer sits between you and the insured bank. Coverage is the FDIC's own $250,000 per depositor per bank, and Treasury bills bought at TreasuryDirect carry no management fee.
The 2024 consent orders that hit banking-as-a-service banks do not touch a deposit held directly at a chartered bank. The 13-week Treasury bill auction of 5 October 2026 cleared at 4.149%, against 3.69% on the Crane 100 money fund index. Running cost is near zero at low balances: Wells Fargo Initiate is $0 with a $2,000 balance, Bank of America Fundamentals charges nothing in the first year, and Navy Federal Business Checking has no monthly fee.

rows.label: 12. Limitations
cells: Idle cash under $250,000 earns nothing, and Treasury's $250,000 minimum rules out most pre-seed companies. Cash cannot be deposited at all, and card spend abroad costs up to 3%. Closures and holds recur in one-star reviews (21% of 2,839 on Trustpilot, 5 October 2026), the Column agreement allows suspension at any time, and in 2024 Mercury gave businesses in listed countries about a month's notice before closing their accounts. Partner-bank changes can alter routing details, and no phone number is published.

Checking earns nothing, and the top 3.91% Treasury rate needs more than $20M; under $500K earns 3.56% after the tiers were cut on 2 October 2026. Access is gated: $50,000 in cash for the monthly card if you have raised money, and a May 2026 user report says a US residential address is now required. Brex told tens of thousands of small businesses to leave in 2022, FINRA fined Brex Treasury $900,000, and Trustpilot sits at 1.9 from 575 reviews. Foreign card spend carries up to a 3% markup, the wire FX margin is undisclosed, and there are no cash deposits or ATM access.

Eligibility is narrow because sole proprietors are not accepted and a US-based owner or US operating address is required. There are no cash deposits and no ATM access. Savings yield is low at up to 1.00% with a $25,000 minimum; higher yield means Treasury, with its $50,000 minimum and 0.60% fee under $2 million. Checking cover is $250,000 in total across sub-accounts. Monthly Terms needs $25,000 at Rho, non-US spend earns no cashback, and Rho Capital requires a personal credit report. No RTP or FedNow, and the API cannot send payments.

Founders outside the US face friction: every owner needs a physical US address, the business needs an operating presence in the US, 31 owner countries are prohibited, and one onboarding page demands an SSN for every beneficial owner. Yield is bought with the subscription: Starter savings pay 1.19%, checking pays nothing, and reaching 3.21% costs $90 a month. No public API, no Zelle, no stated RTP or FedNow, and unpublished transaction limits.

Yield is close to zero: checking earns nothing and the savings accounts pay 0.01% to 0.02% APY (2 October 2026). Fees add up for an online-first startup: $25 per outgoing domestic wire, $40 per outgoing international wire, $15 per incoming wire unless the sender used Chase, a 3% foreign card adjustment, $34 overdrafts, and 1% up to $25 per Same Day ACH or Real Time Payment. Onboarding is restrictive for remote founders: multi-member LLCs need every member in a branch, and the pages do not confirm that a foreign address is accepted. Coverage stops at $250,000 per entity with no sweep. Trustpilot scores it 1.3, and no accounting integration or business API is confirmed.

Onboarding is a sales process with no published time to open, and current pages do not state SSN, ITIN, address or entity rules; the only document that does dates from 2021. Yield is thin below $50,000, where the money market pays 0.10% APY (30 September 2026) and checking pays nothing, and standard FDIC coverage is $250,000 unless you enrol in Insured Cash Sweep, whose yields and fees are not published. Costs stack past the Essentials bundle: $32 maintenance, $0.15 per ACH, $40 a month for online ACH, $25 per international wire and $30 daily overdrafts.

Coverage stops at $250,000 per bank for the whole corporation; every dollar above that needs another bank, another login and another feed, or an IntraFi placement whose cost is not published. Wires cost $30 to $45 each at Wells Fargo and Bank of America, and foreign-currency wires carry an unpublished exchange markup. At the two example big banks, founders outside the US are blocked: Bank of America says foreign business customers are unable to apply and Wells Fargo rejects registered-agent and virtual addresses. Entry-level checking pays 0% to 0.01%, reconciliation is manual, and the sources used here do not quantify the hours this route takes each month.

rows.label: Choose this if you are…
cells:
Ideal for: US-formed startups paying by ACH or wire that want $0 fees plus deep FDIC coverage.
Best when: you either hold under $250,000 and accept zero interest, or hold $250,000 or more and will put it in Mercury Treasury; your founders may live abroad; and you value free domestic and USD international wires, a no-guarantee 1.5% cashback charge card and an API.
Avoid if: you need cash deposits, interest on small balances or a published phone line, or a founder lives in a country on Mercury's prohibited list.

Ideal for: funded US startups that want corporate cards with spend software plus insured cash.
Best when: you hold $50,000 or more, an owner can be verified at a US physical address, and you will park idle cash in Treasury (3.56% to 3.91% as of 5 October 2026) rather than leave it in no-yield checking.
Avoid if: you are bootstrapped with a thin balance, run the company from abroad on a virtual address, need cash deposits or instant payment rails, or cannot tolerate a provider that has cut off small accounts before.

Ideal for: US-incorporated startups with a US-based owner wanting $0 wires plus 24/7 support.
Best when: you hold $25,000 or more at Rho, pay vendors by ACH and wire, and will use Treasury or the Platinum card rather than savings interest.
Avoid if: you are a sole proprietor, have no US-based owner or US operating address, handle cash, need an API that can send money, or need instant payments, since RTP and FedNow are not documented.

Ideal for: US-based founders who want many free checking accounts with clean bookkeeping.
Best when: your company is a US-registered LLC or C-corp whose owners have US addresses and SSNs or passports, you move money mostly by ACH and domestic wire, and you want a $0 account with accountant access rather than treasury yield or an API.
Avoid if: you live outside the US without a US address, you hold large idle cash that needs Treasury bill yield, you need an API or instant payment rails, or an unexplained account freeze would stop your business.

Ideal for: US-based founders who want a big chartered bank with a branch plus Ink credit cards.
Best when: you can hold $2,000 in checking to waive the fee, bank in person when needed, and keep idle cash elsewhere for yield.
Avoid if: you live outside the US, run a multi-member LLC without branch access, or need treasury yield and a documented accounting sync from the start.

Ideal for: VC-track tech startups that want deposits at a chartered bank plus in-house credit.
Best when: you keep $15,000 or more on deposit, plan a priced round, and want venture debt and a charge card from the same bank that holds your cash.
Avoid if: you need same-day self-serve opening, a published current policy for founders without an SSN or US address, or yield on balances under $50,000, which pay 0.10% APY as of 30 September 2026.

Ideal for: US-resident founders holding under $250,000 with few payments plus time to spare.
Best when: you want deposits directly at a chartered bank, can keep a $2,000 to $5,000 balance to waive the monthly fee, and will buy Treasury bills and reconcile the books yourself.
Avoid if: you live outside the US, hold more than $250,000 at one bank, send several wires a month, or need per-employee card rules beyond a daily cap.
